token_classes_note: Order is load-bearing: FINGERPRINT must precede NUMBER (most fingerprints start with a digit, and NUMBER would otherwise split "@3f9c2d" into a number and a name at the first letter), and OP must follow NAME.

token_classes.name: COMMENT
token_classes.note: a line comment, from # to end of line

token_classes.name: FINGERPRINT
token_classes.note: A rule fingerprint -- @ plus exactly six hex characters -- has to be its own token, ahead of NUMBER and NAME: most fingerprints start with a digit, and NUMBER would otherwise split "@3f9c2d" into a number and a name at the first letter.

token_classes.name: NUMBER
token_classes.note: an integer or decimal literal; parsed exactly, never as a float

token_classes.name: STRING
token_classes.note: a double-quoted string; four escape sequences are recognized inside it -- \" \\ \n \t -- resolved to their code point at token construction (lexer.py), no others; the regex here only finds the string's extent (an escaped quote does not close it, so a trailing backslash right before what looks like a closing quote leaves the string unterminated), it does not itself validate which two-character escape is legal

token_classes.name: NAME
token_classes.note: an identifier, hyphen-joined segments allowed (e.g. derives-from)

token_classes.name: OP
token_classes.note: `@` also appears in OP, as a fallback: a malformed fingerprint (wrong length, non-hex characters) then tokenizes as a lone '@' the parser can catch and name the fix for, rather than silently vanishing.

keyword_categories.statement-shape: the shape of a statement -- the parser must see these to know what kind of statement it is reading
keyword_categories.operators-and-connectives: connectives and operator-like words that are not spellable as punctuation
keyword_categories.literals: the three literal values that are words rather than syntax
keyword_categories.distinctive-syntax: operations with distinctive syntax the parser must recognise
keyword_categories.rule-plane: a compile-time-only constraint, never executed (unbound v2.0 section 33)

keywords_note: Reserved words are only those that carry structure: a word the parser must see to know the shape of a statement. Everything else that used to be a keyword -- count, text, lower, upper, whole, ask, read -- is now an ordinary builtin function, callable as `count of xs` exactly like a user's own `detail of id`, and shadowable by a user function of the same name. test_names.py enforces the ceiling: every word NOT in this set must work as a function name, and the ceiling itself (32) is argued word-by-word in that file's docstring.
builtins_note: Builtins are ordinary functions, not keywords. The parser only needs their names so a bare `count of xs` is read as a call rather than a variable; it does not need to know what they do. A user may define a function with the same name, and theirs is the one that runs (test_names.py's test_user_definition_shadows_a_builtin). Every builtin in this language is unary -- one argument, via `of` or juxtaposition -- so arity is 1 across the board.

builtins.name: count
builtins.note: shadowable by a user function of the same name

builtins.name: lower
builtins.note: shadowable by a user function of the same name

builtins.name: upper
builtins.note: shadowable by a user function of the same name

builtins.name: text
builtins.note: shadowable by a user function of the same name

builtins.name: whole
builtins.note: shadowable by a user function of the same name

builtins.name: ask
builtins.note: shadowable by a user function of the same name

builtins.name: read
builtins.note: shadowable by a user function of the same name

builtins.name: normalize
builtins.note: shadowable by a user function of the same name; NFC form; never an effect kind

builtins.name: join
builtins.note: concatenates a list of text into one string, in order, in O(n); no separator argument (a separator is for-each's job); an empty list joins to the empty string; a non-text element is an error, never a silent coercion; shadowable by a user function of the same name; never an effect kind

builtins.name: sine
builtins.note: shadowable by a user function of the same name; takes DEGREES, consistent with the drawing protocol's `rotate` -- degrees are whole numbers and stay exact under this language's arithmetic, where radians would arrive already approximated; the only operation in the language that returns an approximate value, and it returns one for EVERY input including `sine of 0` -- the operation's true result being representable at one argument does not make the operation exact

builtins.name: rest
builtins.note: the list without its first element; lists only (for a text prefix use `first n of`); the rest of an empty list is an error, not a silent empty list; shadowable by a user function of the same name; never an effect kind

effect_kinds_note: The closed vocabulary of effect kinds, grouped by boundary. Lives here, rather than in shapes.py where it originated, because the parser also needs it -- to validate a rule's effect kind at parse time -- and parser.py cannot import shapes.py (shapes.py imports parser.py; the reverse would be a cycle). Closed is the point: an open vocabulary cannot be searched or diffed across packages, and duplicating it in two files would let the two copies drift.
field_name_token_kinds_note: Field names a record literal, with-clause, or when-pattern entry may use -- a field name is not a position where a keyword can be structural, since records nest arbitrarily (v2.0 section 35) and a field may be named `first`, `to`, or any other ordinary word that happens to double as a keyword elsewhere. NAME is included: a field may always be an ordinary, non-reserved word.
positional_words_note: Six words are load-bearing grammar, read positionally at exactly one site each, and deliberately kept OUT of `keywords` above to protect the reserved-word ceiling test_names.py enforces. This section is descriptive only -- the parser does not consult it; each word is still matched positionally in its own parse_* method, exactly as before. It exists because no other table in the repository records these words as grammar at all.

positional_words.note: Neither `may` nor `not` is reserved for this: `not` already carried logical negation and needed no new grant, and `may` is read positionally inside parse_rule only, so a program that never writes `rule` still has `may` free as an ordinary name.

`is` is read positionally, right here, only -- like `may` in parse_rule -- so a program that never writes `is nothing` still has `is` free as an ordinary name. Requiring NOTHING to follow (rather than accepting bare `is` unconditionally) is what lets `when subject is { ... }` use the same word positionally, one level up in parse_when, without parse_comparison's loop swallowing it first.

positional_words.attaches_to: a trailing rationale on an Assign or Rule
positional_words.note: read positionally, right here, only -- like `may` and `is` -- so it stays free as an ordinary name everywhere else (test_names.py's reserved-word ceiling; test_annotation.py confirms `because` stays out of KEYWORDS).

positional_words.attaches_to: a rule's override clause, naming the earlier rule it replaces
positional_words.note: matched via `self.at("NAME", "supersedes")`; positional like the others, so it never needed a reservation.
matched by peeking for the literal word `note` immediately followed by `:`; test_annotation.py confirms `note` stays out of KEYWORDS.

positional_words.attaches_to: one entry inside a note block, naming the rule it derives from
positional_words.note: matched via `self.at("NAME", "derives-from")`; positional like the others.
